best_field_traits: Look for tall wetland stems with long leaves and large feathery flower heads.
The flower head contains many small spikelets, each with several florets and conspicuous silky hairs.
Check the leaf collar and mature spikelet to distinguish common reed from giant reed (Arundo).
Texas has native, Gulf Coast and introduced Phragmites lineages. A common-reed ID does NOT tell you which lineage it is.
Strong reed-like perennial: upright tall jointed culms, broad linear leaves, underground rhizomes, feathery panicles, and multi-flowered spikelets with silky rachilla hairs
Species-level identification: inspect a true multi-flowered spikelet with long silky rachilla hairs, not a single tuft or simply 'cane'

Native-lineage americanus often has shiny smooth red-brown exposed late-season stems, older sheaths readily loose/caducous, generally ligules 1.0–1.7 mm; long glumes often lower 3–6.5 and upper 5.5–11 mm
Introduced Eurasian lineage often has duller/ridged stems and persistent tightly clasping leaf sheaths, ligules 0.4–0.9 mm, lower glumes 2.5–5.0 and upper 4.5–7.5 mm; these measurements overlap

Gulf Coast berlandieri lineage is additional concern in Texas/southern U.S.; its historical origin and taxonomy are treated differently by USGS and Kew; morphology/genetics and provenance may be required
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Whole reed colony, flowering panicle and wetland habitat with scale; compare stand structure but do not decide native from density
SAME LIVE culm near mid-stem: shiny or ridged exposed internode with node, aging leaf sheath wrapped or gaping, and true collar

5–10 intact mature ligules from leaves near the middle third of several culms, short ciliate fringe included but stray long hairs excluded; photograph the membranous junction with a 1-mm rule and record center + both lateral measurements.
Five ripe matched lower and upper glumes detached with accurate 1-mm ruler; annotate each glume separately
Silky spikelet/rachilla hairs, fertile lemma and flowering head macros; compare Arundo donax and Zizaniopsis miliacea
Document locality and collect voucher or DNA/haplotype evidence for disputed Gulf / native / Eurasian lineages BEFORE treatment
crew_field_check: FIRST: is it the species common reed? Look for large silky feathery panicles and true reed leaf/sheath with multi-flowered spikelets; compare Arundo donax and Zizaniopsis miliacea.
NEXT: a species-level Phragmites ID is NOT an invasive designation. Texas has native americanus, introduced Eurasian and disputed-origin Gulf Coast berlandieri lineages.
On SAME mature culm, compare sheath detachment, smooth reddish glossy versus dull ridged exposed stem, and measure ligule (native often 1–1.7 mm, introduced often 0.4–0.9).
At 10–20× measure lower and upper ripe glumes (americanus generally longer; actual distributions overlap). Count 3–4 independent traits; winter photo and panicle colors alone do not suffice.
Photograph both flower and vegetative parts, season/locality, and consult a knowledgeable herbarium or genotype for ambiguous Gulf Coast or management-critical records.
Do not spray/mow as exotic solely on a big stand or seedhead: label Phragmites australis, lineage undetermined until actually verified.

comparisons.key_distinctions: TWO DIFFERENT TASKS: (A) Species identity: Phragmites australis versus Arundo donax and Zizaniopsis miliacea using real spikelets, rachilla/lemma hair placement, and floral architecture. (B) Lineage: subsp. americanus (North American native), Eurasian introduced subsp. australis (often invasive), and Gulf Coast subsp. berlandieri (Kew accepted/native Texas; historical cryptogenic assessments differ). FIRST compare old sheaths and culm surface, THEN repeat true ligule and paired mature glume measurements from multiple culms. Gulf Coast can mimic Eurasian morphology; inconclusive Texas specimens remain LINEAGE UNRESOLVED pending voucher/lineage testing. Photos labelled only Phragmites australis prove species-level organs, NOT subspecies.

measured_species_reproductive_key_202610.status: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — source-backed species-level reproductive anatomy; lineage identity NOT certified
measured_species_reproductive_key_202610.look_here_first: First verify COMMON REED by dissecting a SILKY, MULTIFLORETED spikelet from a branched plume: persistent unequal glumes below, a lowest sterile or staminate floret, and multiple fertile florets borne along a long-white-hairy rachilla. This establishes species-group morphology, NOT native versus invasive lineage.
measured_species_reproductive_key_202610.measured_growth_and_collar: Rhizomatous perennial reed; AusGrass reports culms ~1–6 m, blades 20–60 cm × 8–32 mm, compound plume ~20–50 cm. True ligule is a short ciliate/fringed MEMBRANE at the inside blade–sheath junction, not the long white spikelet hairs. For lineage work, replicate measurements on 5–10 Texas leaves: native americanus often ~1.0–1.7 mm versus Eurasian introduced ~0.4–0.9 mm, with overlap and Gulf Coast lineage as an additional unresolved possibility.
measured_species_reproductive_key_202610.measured_spikelet_and_florets: Pedicelled laterally compressed spikelet ~10–18 mm (AusGrass and USDA APHIS). One basal STERILE OR STAMINATE floret, then generally (2–)3–10(–11) fertile florets and sometimes reduced distal florets; do not label every scale a separate spikelet. Mature units break apart ABOVE persistent basal glumes and between fertile florets. Photograph rachilla and one intact lower-to-upper floret sequence.
measured_species_reproductive_key_202610.measured_glumes: Two persistent unequal lanceolate glumes; lower ~3–7 mm, upper ~5–9(10) mm in AusGrass/USDA APHIS. These are broad species-level ranges, not lineage-specific thresholds. For comparative lineage screening on local specimens, the existing native americanus ~3–6.5 / 5.5–11 mm and introduced Eurasian ~2.5–5 / 4.5–7.5 mm ranges OVERLAP. Separate and measure glumes on multiple same-population mature spikelets; do not infer them from an overview photograph.
measured_species_reproductive_key_202610.measured_lemma_palea_callus_awn: Fertile lemma ~8–15 mm across USDA APHIS/AusGrass, narrow, thin, usually 1–3-veined, long-acuminate but WITHOUT a true long awn; palea ~3–4 mm, two-veined. The conspicuous silky white plume hairs (~5–14 mm in AusGrass) grow on the elongated FLORET CALLUS / rachilla, NOT over the lemma face. A pointed lemma tip is not proof of an awn. Separate lowest sterile-floret lemma from fertile lemma before annotating.
measured_species_reproductive_key_202610.local_lookalikes: Arundo donax: tall cane and soft plume too, but spikelet florets/lemma hair placement and sheath/collar anatomy differ; do not decide by height. Zizaniopsis miliacea: coarse marsh grass with distinct male and female ONE-FLORET spikelets on the same branched head, versus Phragmites' several florets along one silky spikelet rachilla. Tripsacum dactyloides: thick jointed male-over-female flowering spikes rather than a fine branched reed plume. None of these comparisons certifies a Phragmites lineage.
crew_id_sequence: 1. LOOK HERE FIRST: photograph connected reed rhizome/crown, leafy culm, complete branched plume; never infer Hays nativity or invasion status from stand size.
2. Open the blade–sheath collar on 5–10 mature Texas leaves; measure actual ciliate membranous ligule with a 1-mm bar, record sheath age and exposed internode texture separately.
3. Isolate 3–5 ripe spikelets at 10–20×: count 2 persistent glumes, basal sterile/staminate floret and 3–11 fertile florets; record whole spikelet length.

4. Separate lower and upper glumes, lower sterile lemma, one fertile lemma and palea with a millimeter ruler. Trace 5–14 mm silky hairs to callus/rachilla rather than falsely labeling lemma pubescence or an awn.

5. Compare Arundo and Zizaniopsis reproductive units at the same scale. Only AFTER species-level verification consider native americanus, introduced Eurasian and Gulf Coast lineage with several independent culm/sheath/ligule/glume characters plus expert voucher/genetics if ambiguous.

6. Management gate: if lineage is unresolved, retain 'Phragmites australis — lineage undetermined'; do not mark native/invasive or recommend removal based on plume, one measurement, or a non-Texas photo.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Common reed: identify the species first, then consider its three Texas lineages
steps: 1 · Spot common reed: tall wetland stems, broad leaves and feathery heads. Use the whole-plant photo first; Arundo can look similar.
2 · Find the real leaf junction (blade, wrapping sheath and small fringed ligule) and an opened spikelet containing several florets.
3 · At species level, Phragmites has silky hairs on the axis between florets. Arundo's silk is mainly associated with lemmas/floret bases. A plume alone won't separate them.
4 · Texas can have native americanus, introduced Eurasian australis and Gulf Coast berlandieri. Inspect several old sheaths and exposed stems; ligule and glume lengths overlap.
5 · Can't establish the lineage? Write 'Phragmites australis — lineage unresolved.' Do not call it invasive or plan removal on the strength of one photograph.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Species first; lineage second. Three Texas lineages may look alike. These teaching photographs do NOT establish Hays County lineage or justify control.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Source-identified Gulf and native reference photos are examples, not Texas genetic vouchers. True Gulf measured inner ligule and paired glume macros are still missing. The photos must not be used alone to declare a stand invasive.
advanced_steps_preserved_20261027: 1 · Confirm this is Phragmites australis rather than Arundo donax or Zizaniopsis miliacea using real mult-flowered spikelets, ciliate ligule, plume and rhizome. The source images establish species-level anatomy, never an invasive lineage.

2 · THREE PHOTO-LABELLED LINEAGES: native americanus Michigan panel 3 and Matt Lavin North Dakota panel 14 (author describes native despite a filename that says australis australis), introduced Eurasian australis Ontario panel 12, Gulf berlandieri Florida panel 13. All photos are source-labelled only, and no genetic or local Texas subspecies identification is verified. Do not compare seasonally unmatched stand density.
3 · Mature sheath: sample several same-season older culms. Native americanus may loosen/shed old sheaths; introduced Eurasian often keeps them attached; Gulf berlandieri can overlap.

4 · Exposed stem: compare older internodes beneath loosened sheaths. Native americanus often smooth, shiny/reddish; introduced often more dull and ridged; Gulf may be reddish/branched. Avoid classification from one stem.

5 · True blade–sheath ligule: open the existing Harry Rose close-up and new Austrian species-only anatomy panels 16 and 17. The new panels show actual inner leaf/sheath junctions, original 5-mm and 10-mm PHOTO SCALES, and visible hair fringes; source plant genotype/lineage is UNCONFIRMED, so DO NOT call a European photo an invasive haplotype or pretend the printed scale bar measures a photographed individual ligule. Obtain matched, measured 5–10 ligules from each lineage-confirmed population to compare native versus introduced; Gulf may overlap. USDA method refinement: use mature leaves from middle third, include short ligule hair fringe but not isolated long hairs, measure center and two sides and average.

6 · Separate lower and upper glumes from several ripe spikelets; photograph the glumes with scale when available, comparing replicates. Existing photographed labels teach organ identity but not a North American haplotype. Avoid confusing the next larger basal sterile-floret lemma with the upper glume; check exact attachment position before recording length (new lesson 12).

7 · Where traits conflict, origin is unclear or control is proposed, mark LINEAGE UNRESOLVED until specimen/herbarium review and necessary genetic work. Do not remove source-native Gulf or americanus reeds based on species-level photos.
8 · Compare nearby look-alikes separately: Arundo donax has its own collar and hairy-lemma illustration clearly marked as NOT Phragmites; these do not establish Phragmites lineage.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · THREE PHRAGMITES LINEAGES — TEXAS
field_id_short_tiles.short: NATIVE americanus vs INTRODUCED Eurasian australis vs GULF COAST berlandieri — do NOT classify from a species-only photo.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Three lineages are important in Texas, not only native vs invasive: (1) P. australis subsp. americanus is North American native; older sheaths loosen/are shed, exposed stems are often smooth and shiny red-brown, and ligules typically ~1.0–1.7 mm. (2) Eurasian P. australis subsp. australis is introduced and frequently invasive; persistent tight sheaths, dull/ridged stems, ligules typically ~0.4–0.9 mm. (3) Gulf Coast subsp. berlandieri occurs in Texas; Kew currently accepts it as NATIVE to Texas, but older USGS accounts describe its historical origin in the southern USA as uncertain/cryptogenic; it may be confused with the introduced form because quantitative characters overlap. Across lineages, compare upper and lower GLUMES from several ripe spikelets and collar measurements from multiple same-population leaves, not just plume color or stand density. Source-labeled Michigan americanus gallery images are native-reference candidates, NOT Hays County vouchers. No existing card photograph is lineage-confirmed by genotype. For a Texas population of management consequence, keep LINEAGE UNRESOLVED until specimen/voucher assessment and, where needed, genetic lineage identification. Peer-reviewed Gulf Coast photo comparison: Kettenring et al. 2012, Fig. 5 contrasts source-labelled berlandieri with introduced Short A, Short B and Delta sublineages, showing why overall reed height/density cannot certify introduced status. Figure is an external study reference, NOT an archived gallery photo or a substitute for genuine sheath/ligule/glume views.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · OLD LEAF SHEATHS — RELEASED VS CLINGING
field_id_short_tiles.short: Inspect a mature culm: older sheaths loosen on many native americanus plants; usually cling on introduced Eurasian plants.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Check several OLD culms in the same season, not tender green spring shoots. Native americanus: senescent sheaths often peel or naturally drop, exposing glossy upper internodes. Introduced Eurasian australis: dry older sheaths often remain tight. Gulf Coast berlandieri: variable and can resemble introduced; a persistent sheath is NOT enough to classify a Texas plant as invasive. Prefer similar-height culms and both naturally attached and loosening sheaths on the same photographed population; record month/date and exact source lineage determination. IMPORTANT SOUTHWESTERN UPDATE (Palmquist et al. 2026): The number of old sheaths retained can change with arid climate and hydrologic regime. Test HOW TIGHTLY mature sheaths clasp the culm, rather than simply counting retained sheath leaves. This Arizona/Utah native-vs-introduced result is not itself a Gulf Coast subspecies test.
field_id_short_tiles.status: SOURCE-VOUCHERED introduced COLLAR close-up now present, but older persistent-sheath sequence and matched Gulf sheath photos still needed.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · EXPOSED CULM SURFACE AND COLOR
field_id_short_tiles.short: Look beneath loosened older sheaths: glossy reddish culms support native americanus; dull ridged culms may support introduced Eurasian reed.
field_id_short_tiles.details: On several late-season culms inspect EXPOSED internodes between nodes. Americanus often has red-brown/purple, smooth, glossy exposed stems. Eurasian australis often duller, greener/tan and finely ridged with tight sheaths. Gulf berlandieri may show woody, branching or reddish stems; these features OVERLAP and colors change with age, light and season. Do not label a stand from a single reddish cane. Photograph mature nodes, sheath scars and an upright stand with the same observer/site/voucher recorded.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · TRUE INNER LIGULE — MULTIPLE MEASUREMENTS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Measure the true short membranous ligule and its short hair fringe; don't measure isolated long hairs.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Open five to ten mature leaf blade/sheath junctions from several culms and show a 1-mm ruler where practical. Published non-Gulf tendencies: native americanus often has a longer ciliate membrane (~1.0–1.7 mm), introduced Eurasian australis shorter (~0.4–0.9 mm); overlapping observations occur. Gulf berlandieri commonly overlaps introduced forms, so the native-versus-introduced ligule rule is NOT a Gulf Coast ID key. The existing Harry Rose collar photograph identifies WHERE to look but has no lineage-confirmed Texas provenance. A sharp unscaled image still teaches organ placement, but not a reliable measured cutoff. MEASUREMENT PROTOCOL: USDA guidance includes the short ciliate fringe of the membranous ligule in ligule height, but excludes isolated long, easily broken hairs. Select mature leaves from the MIDDLE THIRD of culms; measure at center plus both lateral portions and average. Do not claim a measured native/introduced difference from the white long hairs in the Burke photograph.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · TWO GLUMES — MEASURE MATURE MATCHED SPIKELETS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Separate lower and upper glumes from ripe spikelets; ranges overlap and need population-level replication.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Remove several ripe attached spikelets from the same vouchered population. For each, photograph the LOWER and UPPER persistent glumes separately at an equal scale. Broad reported lower/upper lengths: americanus approximately 3–6.5 and 5.5–11 mm; introduced Eurasian australis approximately 2.5–5 and 4.5–7.5 mm. These are approximate published diagnostic tendencies, NOT proof from any one glume, and they do not reliably classify Gulf berlandieri. The Harry Rose annotated source images currently show which organs are glumes, but were not assigned to a genetically confirmed lineage; do not back-assign their dimensions. PHOTO TRAP: locate the two persistent basal glumes first; the next longer bract may be the lower sterile-floret lemma, not the upper glume. Do not measure a sterile lemma as a glume and accidentally assign a native lineage.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 07 · DECISION AND MANAGEMENT HOLD
field_id_short_tiles.short: If several independent traits agree, record a tentative lineage; if Gulf overlap or management consequences remain, leave it LINEAGE UNRESOLVED.
field_id_short_tiles.details: STEP 1: Verify Phragmites species via flowering/glume/rachilla anatomy and distinguish Arundo donax or Zizaniopsis miliacea. STEP 2: Consider all three Texas possibilities: native americanus, introduced Eurasian australis, and Gulf berlandieri. STEP 3: Photograph and document the same population's old sheaths, exposed culms, at least 5–10 true ligules and several paired ripe glumes; capture season/locality and collection/voucher where permitted. STEP 4: Check multiple characters together. If traits conflict, if Gulf Coast overlap is plausible, or before a removal decision, seek regional botanist/herbarium advice and molecular haplotype/genetic confirmation when necessary. Species-only pictures never certify a lineage; Kew treats berlandieri native to Texas while some historical treatments considered Gulf origin uncertain. NEW SOUTHWEST RESEARCH (Palmquist et al., 2026): Genetically tested native and introduced reeds from the greater Grand Canyon region showed considerable native morphological variation. Hairy axillary buds and loose sheath clasping helped distinguish them there; a published basal ligule height distinction should not be confused with the total fringed ligule lengths in the older three-way key. This regional result should NOT be transplanted as a diagnostic key for Gulf Coast berlandieri. Never authorize invasive-control action based on one clue.
field_id_short_tiles.status: FIELD DECISION KEY READY — local lineage identification scientifically held pending confirmed provenance/genetics

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 08 · RHIZOMES, STEMS AND TRUE COLLAR
field_id_short_tiles.short: Tall rhizomatous perennial; short fringed membranous ligule inside blade–sheath junction
field_id_short_tiles.details: Published species-level culms often ~1–6 m, blades ~20–60 cm by 8–32 mm, branched plume ~20–50 cm. Open the true collar: the ciliate membrane is NOT the long white hairs of the spikelet. Existing archived collar panels 2 and 6 are not lineage-confirmed Texas vouchers. Measure 5–10 leaves at 1-mm scale before comparing lineages.
field_id_short_tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — REPLICATED TEXAS LIGULES AND ROOTED CULM

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 09 · TWO UNEQUAL PERSISTENT GLUMES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Lower glume commonly ~3–7 mm; upper ~5–9(10) mm, measured on mature spikelets
field_id_short_tiles.details: These AusGrass/USDA APHIS values are broad species-level measurements, not a native-versus-introduced cutoff. Lower and upper glume ranges overlap between North American lineages; dissect 3–5 ripe Texas spikelets, separate each glume, label which is lower/upper, and photograph at 10–20× with a millimeter scale. No existing panorama proves these dimensions.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 10 · LEMMA, PALEA AND HAIR INSERTION
field_id_short_tiles.short: Fertile lemma ~8–15 mm, palea ~3–4 mm; conspicuous silky hairs grow from callus/rachilla
field_id_short_tiles.details: A fertile lemma is narrow and pointed but lacks a conspicuous true long awn; a sharp lemma tip is NOT itself an awn. Published silky rachilla/callus hairs ~5–14 mm create the plume. Open a ripe spikelet, distinguish the basal sterile-floret lemma, fertile lemma and two-veined palea, and trace hair origins with a 1-mm bar before drawing microscopic arrows.
field_id_short_tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — 10–20× HAIR INSERTION AND FLORET DISSECTION

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 11 · SEPARATE ARUNDO AND GIANT CUTGRASS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Compare WHERE hairs grow and whether spikelets are multifloreted or sex-separated
field_id_short_tiles.details: Giant reed (Arundo donax) also has broad canes and a plume, but much of its silky hair is associated with the lemma/floret base rather than Phragmites' long hairy rachilla. Giant cutgrass (Zizaniopsis miliacea) bears separate male and female one-flowered spikelets, not several fertile florets along one silky spikelet axis. Eastern gamagrass has thick sex-divided jointed spikes, not a fine branched plume. Require matched, public-rights spikelet dissections before final ID or management.
field_id_short_tiles.status: FIELD COMPARISON — MATCHED REPRODUCTIVE MACROS MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 12 · GLUME TRAP — DON'T MEASURE THE BASAL STERILE LEMMA
field_id_short_tiles.short: Two glumes are at the spikelet base. The next longer bract can be a sterile-floret lemma, NOT an oversized upper glume.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Start at the stalk/pedicel attachment of an intact ripe spikelet. Locate the short LOWER glume and the somewhat longer UPPER glume—the two persistent bracts at the base. The next bract above them can be the conspicuous lemma of a basal sterile or staminate floret, commonly longer (about 8–15 mm) and sometimes mistaken for the upper glume. Never use that lemma length to conclude native americanus. Confirm which bract attaches where, gently separate the glumes from at least five mature spikelets, photograph each with a 1-mm scale and calculate replicated lengths. The current Harry Rose annotated spikelet shows labelled glumes and florets but is SPECIES-LEVEL and cannot prove any one lineage. If uncertain, leave lineage unresolved; Gulf berlandieri can overlap introduced measurements.
field_id_short_tiles.status: CREW MISIDENTIFICATION TRAP ADDED — EXISTING ANNOTATED ORGAN PHOTO; NO NEW LINEAGE-CERTIFIED GLUME MACROS

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 13 · GULF-COAST TRAP — SHORT LIGULE DOES NOT MEAN INTRODUCED
field_id_short_tiles.short: A short true ligule plus a smooth, shiny older culm can indicate Gulf Coast berlandieri; a dull, ridged culm supports introduced Eurasian reed. Neither character confirms lineage alone.
field_id_short_tiles.details: USDA NRCS's published Saltonstall–Hauber three-lineage key first distinguishes typically longer-ligule americanus from both short-ligule Gulf Coast berlandieri and introduced Eurasian reed. The second branch suggests berlandieri when older exposed culms are smooth and shiny in the southern range, versus ridged and dull introduced culms. BUT these are tendencies on adequately mature, comparable plants, not a photographic or morphological genotype test. The Gulf Coast and introduced lineages overlap in ligule and mature lower/upper glume dimensions. The new Pensacola Gulf reference photo (panel 19) shows where the external sheaths attach but DOES NOT expose the true inner ligule or prove glossiness of a mature sheath-free internode. The Bonita Springs panel (20) teaches flowering architecture, not lineage-confirming glume measurements. Photograph and measure 5–10 mature inner ligules and paired ripe glumes from the SAME documented stand; include season, site and voucher. If any character conflicts or management decisions depend on it, use specialist/herbarium review and appropriate molecular haplotype testing. A green outer sheath, a plume or short hairs alone NEVER confirm Eurasian invasive reed. SUPPORTING GULF STUDY: Williams et al. (2012) used genetic assays on southeastern populations, illustrating Gulf smooth/shiny culms and open/drooping panicles against introduced ribbed/dull culms and compact/erect panicles in their Figure 2. This supports multi-character recognition, not diagnosis from one unvouchered Texas plant. Their sample-mean ligule lengths were not significantly different between the Gulf and introduced groups; glume distributions overlapped. The research figure is linked, not licensed for website reproduction.

beginner_learning_path.title: Common reed — four photographs to get oriented
beginner_learning_path.intro: First learn to recognize Phragmites as a species. Then learn its leaf junction and flowers. Only afterward consider whether a Texas stand is native, Gulf Coast, or introduced.
beginner_learning_path.memory_rule: Tall wetland reed → feathery plume → tiny hairy, many-flowered spikelets → lineage needs extra evidence.

steps.title: 1 · Recognize the whole reed
steps.look_for: See the tall, leafy, jointed wetland stems and feathery branching flower heads. This is the whole-plant view to remember.
steps.why_it_matters: A similar tall reed may be Arundo, so use the next two views instead of deciding from height or fluffiness.

steps.title: 2 · Find where a leaf joins the stem
steps.look_for: The broad leaf blade meets a wraparound sheath. At the inner junction is a small, pale, hair-fringed ligule (a little flap). Follow the existing visible arrows.
steps.why_it_matters: The collar confirms part of the grass anatomy, but a hairy ligule alone does NOT determine a native or introduced Phragmites lineage.

steps.title: 3 · Open one tiny part of the plume
steps.look_for: This source-labeled photograph shows a spikelet (a small flowering unit) with two basal glumes and several florets. The silky hairs on the spikelet axis help separate Phragmites from Arundo.
steps.why_it_matters: Use the photographer's existing labels. Do not confuse a long sterile-floret lemma with an upper glume, and do not infer lineage from an unvouchered close-up.

steps.title: 4 · Texas lineage check: don't guess
steps.look_for: This source-identified Gulf Coast Florida photo shows connected stems and outer leaf sheaths. It does NOT show a measured inner ligule or genetically prove the reed is Gulf Coast.
steps.why_it_matters: There are three important regional groups: North American native americanus, introduced Eurasian australis and Gulf Coast berlandieri. Their visible characters overlap. Record 'lineage unknown' when uncertain.
